Messages.Body:
Howdy,

Without going into much detail well let's just say that after each
EC usually comes a time of contemplation for me on the time limits
and the implications they have on the game, especially the finals.

It helps to start this contemplation that out of the 3 "main events"
at Göteborg all 3 timed out. I couldn't help but wonder in at least
one case how the game would've turned out if not for the time limit.

The obvious solution seems to be longer time limits for the finals.
2.5, 3, 4, 5 hour finals time limits are technically possible
(though are probably prone to having logistics difficulties of
their own both for the venue and the players who travel).

I was considering, though, whether it would make sense to introduce a
relative time limit for the finals - e.g. keep the 2 hours but also
count the number of turns, and if the 2-hour time limit is reached,
the game only ends when (say) 15 turns have been completed.

Now this doesn't make it impossible for players to play in a way that
maximizes their strategic advantages with respect to the time limit
as well. There are decks that are getting stronger as turns pass.
Probably some recursion techs might also be more common with this
hybrid system. It gives advantage to decks that take long with their
turns.

Still, I expect this would speed up the game in the sense that even
though some finals might last longer than 2 hours, the amount of
"action" happening per final might be more, and more finals would
be decided by decisive play and less by time-outs.

I don't know if the tournament rules allow the organiser to set such
a relative time limit, but if yes I might consider experimenting
with it to see whether it really has the desired effect. Even before
that I'd like to hear whether anyone has some constructive comments
to this (I'm still scared from implementing 5-hour time limits for
the finals just to speed up things simply because if a game does
reach time, I'm gonna face some interesting situations with the
venue, the players and last but not least the wife...).

So I'm kind of open to comments... :)

--
Regards,

Daneel

I'll just have to disagree on this one, partly. Yes, ignoring the time
and trying to stop all ousts that aren't by you very often is bad
play. No disagreement on that.

However, it being bad play doesn't stop people from doing it, and what
we saw (again) at the EC finals were people trying actively to stall
the game, because they were in a position where they couldn't get a
VP, but didn't want to give VPs to anyone else either (because of
general standings issues, or whatever). Some people are so obsessed
with winning and ranking score issues that they'll do pretty much
anything for those goals. Including "bad play" that leads games to
timeouts.

With no time limits (on finals), those people would be forced to
either self-oust or do a desperate lunge/deal for that VP; that choice
of "just stall until timeout" doesn't exists anymore and stalling
becomes simply stupid and annoying, instead of just annoying.

For practical reasons, the preliminary rounds need time limits, or
course. But in my opinion the final round would get *much* better (and
probably faster) play if there was no time limit at all, or if it was
so long that judges could easily catch and give warnings for stalling,
because so huge amounts of it would be required.

Face it, people. All 3 final rounds at the EC stalled out. There's a
problem here. Maybe this was just because of some specific players
involved in those rounds, but maybe it's a more general problem where
stalling the game to timeout can seem like a valid choice for some
mindsets.

rather than making the finals longer, to remove all "previous standings"

The problem isn't really the time limit--it is the concrete incentive
for some players to have the game time out.

This seems like a nifty idea by itself. The only real seeding
benefits are choosing your seat and tiebreaking. At a large
tournament, or if you happen to be at slow-ish tables, you totally
lose out on the former benefit if you don't know much/anything about
the other finalists' decks.

I'd go with option A above, and work it thusly:

Fifth seed seats herself.
Fourth seed may ask fifth a single Monocle (Yes/No) question - with
all finalists listening to both question and answer - then seats
herself.
Third seed gets to ask fifth a question, then fourth, then seats
herself.
Second seed gets to ask fifth, fourth, third questions, then seats
herself.
First seed gets to ask each lower seed a question (in order, and, as
always, with everyone listening), and then seats herself.

Fifth seed has the no benefit, as always. First seed, OTOH, has up to
four facts about fifth seed's deck, three about fourth, two about
third, and one about second before making her choice, while her deck
remains unknown. Plus everyone has heard what questions are important
to the askers; if someone is asking about bounce, it's a good bet they
have significant bleed.

> Of course, there will be players that already know everything about an
> opponents deck from previous rounds or other scources. This is a
> problem.

Not a big one, IMO. It is unavoidable that some finalists will have
been at the same table with other finalists, or otherwise have a good
sense of what they are playing. More power to them. It's the players
who have done really well but know nothing about the other finalists'
decks who are really losing out. Rather than encourage them to scout
(lame), why not just build in a failsafe?

Alex

Not, however, in tournaments, where winners are required.

- Individual games in the English divisions (where there are around 40
games per team per year, one home and one away for each of the
20-ish clubs in the same division) can end in a win for either
side, or a tie. (3 points for a win, 1 for a tie, 0 for lose.
Ties on number of points are settled on goal difference.)

- Some tournaments (particularly at the level of clubs, rather than
countries) can have a home leg and an away leg, even at the
level of quarter-finals and such. (These are the sort of
tournaments that take place over the space of a year, with a
couple of months between each round.) Other tournaments can
also have replays because you have time to schedule them.

- Many major international tournaments have a "group" stage, where the
clubs/countries that qualified are put into a group of 4 or so
clubs, who play against each other as above. The top two go
through, or something similar.

- Then you get into things like semi-finals of the World Cup, which have
to be decided in order to get someone in the finals. Basically,
any round in a knockout stage of a tournament that takes place
over a short period of time doesn't have time to schedule new
games for ties, you MUST have an outright winner.

- The first way of resolving ties involves 30 minutes of extra time
after the normal 90 minutes. Canonically, after the full 30
minutes, if one side is the winner, they win. However, there
are also variations such as the golden goal (whichever side
scores first in extra time wins, so the other team doesn't have
chance to equalize) or the silver goal (if there's a winner
after the first 15 minutes, they win, otherwise you change ends
and play the second 15 minutes).

- After that, you go to a penalty shoot-out. Five players on each side
take penalties (put ball on ground in front of goal, must score
goal from that kick). Whoever scores most wins. If that's
tied, then you get to do things like sudden death penalties - if
my team scores and yours doesn't on any given pair of penalties
after the initial 5, my team wins.

The point being, soccer is only happy with ties when a winner isn't
"needed".

currently determine a winner) and then 4 finalists, regardless of the

coming in 2nd.

On Aug 11, 7:06 pm, Daneel <dan...@eposta.hu> wrote:
> Howdy,
>
> Without going into much detail well let's just say that after each
> EC usually comes a time of contemplation for me on the time limits
> and the implications they have on the game, especially the finals.
>

Yeah. Continental Championships that don't go to time seem to be
exception rather than the rule. I too think this is unfortunate and
have long been an advocate of 2.5 time limit for finals - I advocate
it for all finals games, but I think it would be especially beneficial
for "big" events and Championships.

To get into the finals at a big tournaments the players (and their
decks) have already demonstrated their ability to get game wins within
2 hours. Yet, we put these top players together at the finals table
and it times out. Why?

In the preliminary rounds you're all implicitly competing with all the
other tables. You either get a GW or you don't. If the table times out
without a GW you all lose.

In the finals, there is always 1 player who is winning, and so has an
incentive to maintain the status quo, and is happy to see slow play,
extended negotiations, and a time-out.

Also, in a high-stakes finals, nobody really wants to stick their neck
out. There's more incentive for canny players to keep their heads down
and see how the table develops.

So, experience tells us that these factors have a tendency to extend
the finals game length beyond the 2 hour mark. I would like to see the
finals have a 2.5 hour length and see if it didn't lead to more finals
ending in a GW. This doesn't require any kind of rules change. I'm not
really sure why event organizers seem so reluctant to do it. I expect
it's mostly habit.

People, have argued that with a longer finals time limit, we can just
expect players to talk more and that game will still time out - it'll
just take longer. Sometimes we'll still get the stalemate, but I would
guess most of the time the extra time will be enough to finish the
game.

My own theory (based on not much evidence) is that a longer time limit
will actually lead to faster play. When there's 10 minutes left
players can start to think about how to hang in there, and slow things
down. If there's still 40 minutes left, at the 100 minute mark,
hanging in there is, often, not a option. You have to figure out how
to win.

-Ben Swainbank

>To be clear, again, the idea is to set up the tournament rules such that
>in the final game, you get a winner by virtue of VPs in the final and
>then preliminary seeding to break ties as always, but places 2-5 are all
>tied, i.e. you get the same prizes and tournament points for 5th place
>as you do 3rd place.

I recommend two slight changes to this. It may seem a little
complicated, but covers the single issue I have with the system.

* Surviving to time is worth 0VP
* When calculating position, all players in the same position use the
worst shared position.

In a 5 player game, this means if all 5 players tie, all players get
5th. If only 1 players scores a VP, they get 1st, and all other
players get 5th. This is how your suggestion currently works.

However, if 2 players gain a VP, according to your system, noone has
won via VP, so all get 0. Or if a player gets 2VP, and another gets 3,
that first player gets no reward for his efforts.

Sure, this brings in the more than real concept of table splitting in
the finals, but at least that'd force the table to move, which is
still the point, no? Better to have a player make a deal and have a
completed table, than try to get it on his own.

The addition I suggest isn't really complicated if you've seen the
current concept used in rankings for ties.

Players C and D tie, and the ranking list is as follows.
1st Player A
2nd Player B
3rd Player C
3rd Player D
5th Player E

My suggestion would make it
1st Player A
2nd Player B
4th Player C
4th Player D
5th Player E

While it looks the same, within the concept of what a finals table
would look like, the limiting factors would mean after the first VP is
taken, anyone who gets a VP is rewarded, even if they can't beat the
eventual winner.

Morgan Vening

If large tournament finals games time out most of the time, then yes,
I'd rather get rid of the finals and simply give the victory to the
biggest winner after 3 rounds. It's better than spending two hours
watching that happen anyway.

Part of the problem is that many finals games are just a formality in
which nothing happens, and most large ones the players can expect the
table to time out. I personally always go to a finals thinking, "I
probably only need 1 VP to win this before it times out." And I would
like for this not to be true.

> > Sit them

> > the other rounds of the tournament work. Watch as folks try to oust
> > folks in the time allotted in the name of actually winning the game.

I happen to support removing the time limits on finals games. But,
for the sake of exploration, we could probably remove the stalemate
with, "Time limit won't stop the finals game until somebody is
ousted." This way, the game couldn't finish with 1/2 for everybody,
and if the game kinda sucked and nobody did anything for 2 hours, then
the game would end as soon as somebody got his ass in gear and ousted
his prey.

And hey, players who regularly maintain that no-limit finals will
result in 5-hour games will probably concede that ONE oust won't take
that long.

> People already do try to oust folks in the time allotted in the name
> of actually winning the game. Seriously. It happens all the time. So
> leaving things the way they are makes sense to me.

Yes, players try to oust. But actual tournament results seem to show
they are much less successful in that than in previous rounds, for
whatever reason. So, if too many finals games are going to time, the
only possible solutions are to change the way the players play, or to
give them more time to play (which I argue will in itself change the
way they play by removing stalling as an option.)

Examine the finals game itself. When someone is ousted:
1 player isn't automatically winning anymore
3 players may lose a place in the final standings
1 player is unaffected

Compare to previous rounds, where there are:
5 players who will lose unless someone is ousted

These two games are clearly constructed differently from the
beginning.

If we want to change the first game to be more like the second, it
means making the stalemate undesirable for all of the players. This
requires ignoring the previous results, or increasing the time limits
to go until someone is ousted. A new arbitrarily long limit, like
2:30, would probably be long enough for someone to be ousted, but
something more direct, like, "Don't stop playing at two hours unless
someone has been ousted" or "There are no time limits in the final"
are both ways that guarantee the stalemate is impossible to achieve
for the player going into the finals in 1st place.

> > > The final table is the chance for 2nd-5th seed players to wrest the
> > > tournament win away from someone who has, on the whole, played better
> > > so far that day. If none of them can do it (or none of them are
> > > willing to do it), just let him walk away with the victory.
>
> > Which is a weird dynamic, compared to the rest of the games in the
> > tournament--why introduce the strange dynamic of "one player gets to win
> > if nothing changes" that is missing from the rest of the tournament?
>
> You can't escape that the finals table will have a different dynamic
> from every other table. It's the only one where the entire tournament
> is on the line.
>
> This particular dynamic is the one that every finals table has ever
> had. And it exists because we a) want to have a final table of VtES
> where the best of the best play against each other for the tournament
> win and we also b) strongly desire there to be a single winner => ties
> must be broken, and we prefer that ties be broken in a manner that
> rewards prior performance, as opposed to just rolling some dice.

I would strongly prefer that ties be broken in a way that rewards
CURRENT performance, than PRIOR performance. But if you're in 1st
place, you may not feel that way. This may be part of why we have
been seeing a hell of a lot of ties in finals games.

If you think prior performance should be more important than current
performance, then please, tell me what that reason is--but I doubt
this is the case. If you'd rather players had a chance in the final
to do well and oust someone, tell me what time limits you think would
be appropriate and why. And if you think 2 hours is enough time, I'd
like to remind you that more finals are timing out every year.

I think, if we're to have an arbitrary time limit, we should keep
track of how long finals games are lasting, and then set the arbitrary
limit to be equal to the time at which 80% of finals games
statistically complete. This way, we should see roughly 80% of finals
games continue to reach completion.

> > If you are doing well, you get into the finals, with gives you the
> > opportunity to A) Win and B) get prizes. Why is it *also* necessary to
> > give first seed the strange motivation that no one else has, and no one
> > else deals with at any other point of the tournament?
>
> Because of a) and b). If you're willing to give up on either one, you
> can alter the dynamic. I'm not.

So, if finals had a two hour time limit, and play only stopped after
the time limit was reached AND someone has been ousted, there would
still be the same tiebreakers as there are now, so players would still
see a definite winner and a definite prize structure. It would
guarantee that just waiting and talking when you're in first place
would not ever win you a tournament, and it would likely not take much
more time to complete than the games we currently have do. I'd like
to hear what you think of that.

-- Brian
